title: Text & Media Connections
keyIdea: A film, a stage play or an audiobook of a story is built from the writer's words. To connect the two versions, find the exact words in the text, then say what the other version kept, what it changed, and how it showed the detail in its own way. A film shows descriptions and feelings with pictures and sound, actors turn stage directions in brackets into actions, and an audiobook reader turns clues such as whispered or BANG! into a voice.
familyTip: After you watch a film of a book you have read, pick one scene together. Open the book at that page. Take turns to name one detail the film kept and one it changed, and read out the words that prove it.

visual.caption: Which version shows the detail this way? Drag each card, or tap it and then a box.

items: “Mira felt small and far from home.”
A close-up of the cat's torn ear
An actor slams a door on cue
The crash of waves on the soundtrack
An actor shivers and rubs her hands

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match shots to sentences, spot what a film kept or changed, follow stage directions, voice an audiobook.

kid: Many stories come in more than one version. There is the book. There may also be a film, a play on a stage, or an audiobook that someone reads aloud. Each one is built from the same words.

To compare them, start with the book. Find the exact words. Then look at the film. Did it keep the detail, or change it? The book says snow, but the film shows rain. That is a change, and you can prove it with the words.
A play script has two kinds of words. Lines are what the actors say. Stage directions sit in brackets, like (slams the door). Actors do not say them. They act them out.

A book can tell you what a character feels. A film has to show it. It uses faces, sounds and how close the camera is. An audiobook reader uses the voice. If the book says she whispered, the reader says it quietly.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. This is the Common Core reading standard RL.4.7: make connections between the text of a story or drama and a visual or oral presentation of the text, identifying where each version reflects specific descriptions and directions in the text. It links to the KS2 National Curriculum in England aims of preparing play scripts to perform and showing understanding through intonation, tone, volume and action.

The lab uses a short lighthouse scene written for it. Learners match four film shots to the exact sentence each one shows, sort six film moments into matches or changes, link four moments on stage to the stage directions they follow, choose a voice for four audiobook lines from clues in the words, and pick the shot that shows a feeling the book only tells.

Common mistakes. Children compare from memory instead of finding the words, so they miss small changes, such as rain for snow or a shout for a whisper. They treat a near match as a match, think stage directions are read aloud, and judge a version as better or worse without pointing to the text. Ask them to quote the words first, then say kept, changed or shown another way.

practice.prompt: Book: “Snow blew in around her boots.” Film: rain pours past her boots. What is this?
practice.hint: Compare the weather word by word. Is snow the same as rain?
practice.explain: The book says snow and the film shows rain, so the film changed this detail.

practice.prompt: MIRA: (rubbing her hands) It is freezing up here. Which words does the actor say out loud?
practice.hint: Words in brackets are stage directions. The name shows who speaks.
practice.explain: Only the line is spoken. The actor acts out (rubbing her hands), and MIRA just shows who is speaking.

practice.prompt: A film scene has {n} details from the book. It keeps {k} of them the same. How many details did it change?
practice.hint: Every detail is either kept or changed. Take the kept ones away.
practice.explain: Kept plus changed makes {n}, so {n} − {k} = {=n-k} details were changed.

practice.prompt: Book: “BANG! A wave hit the rocks below.” How should the audiobook reader say BANG?
choices: Slowly, one letter at a time
practice.hint: Look at the capital letters and the exclamation mark.
practice.explain: Capitals and an exclamation mark are clues for a loud, sudden sound, so the reader says BANG loudly.

practice.prompt: A play script page has {d} stage directions and {s} spoken lines. How many of these does the audience hear the actors say?
practice.hint: Stage directions are acted out, not spoken.
practice.explain: Only the {s} spoken lines are said out loud. The {d} stage directions become actions.

pool.prompt: Book: “an old grey cat with one torn ear”. Film: an old grey cat with two perfect ears. What changed?
pool.hint: Check each describing word in the book against the film.
pool.explain: Old and grey both match. The book says one torn ear, but the film shows perfect ears, so the ear changed.

pool.prompt: Which of these is a stage direction?
pool.explain: (Biscuit jumps onto the table.) is in brackets and tells the actors what happens. The others are spoken lines.

pool.prompt: Book: “Mira felt small and far from home.” Which film shot shows this best?
choices: Tiny Mira alone on a tall tower, dark sea all round
pool.hint: Which shot makes her look small and alone?
pool.explain: A wide shot with tiny Mira alone shows small and far from home. Laughing with friends shows the opposite.

pool.prompt: You want to compare a film scene with the book. What should you do first?
choices: Find the exact words in the book
pool.hint: You need proof for every kept or changed detail.
pool.explain: Find the words first. Memory slips, and the words are your proof that a detail was kept or changed.

pool.prompt: Book: “The light flashed… then nothing.” What should the audiobook reader do at the three dots?
pool.hint: Three dots show that something stops or trails off.
pool.explain: The three dots, called an ellipsis, are a clue to pause before reading then nothing.

pool.prompt: Book: “Mira whispered.” Film: Mira shouts. Which is the best way to describe this?
choices: The film changed a whisper into a shout
pool.hint: The book is the starting point. What did the film do to it?
pool.explain: The book says whispered and the film shows a shout, so the film changed how Mira speaks.

pool.prompt: Book: “Her heart thumped.” How could a film show this?
choices: A close-up of her face with a loud heartbeat sound
pool.hint: A thumping heart means she is scared or excited.
pool.explain: A close-up face and a loud heartbeat show her fear. A yawn or calm music shows the opposite.

pool.prompt: On stage, the keeper keeps polishing the lamp with his back to Mira. Which direction is he following?
pool.hint: Find the direction about the keeper and the lamp.
pool.explain: (not looking up from the lamp) tells the keeper to keep his eyes on the lamp, which is what he acts out.

pool.prompt: A film keeps {k} details from a book scene and changes {c}. How many details did you check?
pool.hint: Each detail you checked was either kept or changed.

pool.prompt: Book: “a small orange light was flashing”. Film: a small orange light flashing far out at sea. What is this?
pool.hint: Check small, orange and flashing one by one.
pool.explain: Small, orange and flashing all appear in the film, so it matches the book.

pool.prompt: A play scene has {s} spoken lines and {d} stage directions. How many parts of the script do the actors turn into actions, not words?
pool.hint: Which parts sit in brackets and are never said aloud?
pool.explain: The {d} stage directions are acted out. The {s} spoken lines are said aloud.
